  ],
  "weaknesses": [

More generally, moving an embedding toward an incorrect class center can increase the proposed geometric-imbalance score while decreasing entropy through confident misclassification.",
    "Theorem 2 conflates imbalance in labeled training samples with neighborhood composition. Subsampling labels on a fixed graph does not imply that minority nodes acquire more majority neighbors; with a fixed encoder and class centers, existing embeddings remain unchanged. A graph-generating model and valid additional assumptions are needed.",
    "The connection between the theory and implementation remains weak. DGIS uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest centroid margin, whereas Definition 1 measures distance to the true class center relative to global separation; no approximation guarantee or direct validation connects them. The ranking explanation is also inaccurate: the confidence weight min(r, 1-r) decreases once r exceeds 0.5. Theorem 3 establishes an algebraic weighting property, not a guarantee of reduced geometric imbalance or pseudo-label error.",

As printed, Tables 1 and 32 give the highest F1 in every setting to configurations marked as excluding both Node-Reordering and DGIS, contradicting the accompanying claim that their combination performs best. Tables 17 and 27 also report different UNREAL results for ostensibly the same ogbn-arxiv setting, including GCN F1 values of 50.32 and 50.65. These inconsistencies prevent confident interpretation of the evidence.",

Appendix B already describes M3S as filtering pseudo-labels through clustering/classifier agreement, closely resembling DPAM, yet the direct comparison is restricted to CS-Random. IceBerg is discussed but not evaluated. Broader comparisons under matched training and tuning budgets would clarify the contribution of the added ranking and filtering mechanisms.",
    "The scalability and reproducibility claims exceed the supplied details. Appendix K omits comparable hyperparameter configurations for ogbn-arxiv/products and does not adequately specify the large-scale sampling setup. Table 12 measures fixed training epochs and selection operations on small graphs, while the complete method can use 100 retraining rounds. End-to-end runtime, peak memory, and matched computational budgets are needed to substantiate the efficiency claims. strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: unreliable pseudo-labels for minority classes in semi-supervised graph learning. The modular framework is practical and avoids synthesizing nodes or edges.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering three GNN architectures, synthetic and natural imbalance, and larger graphs. Reported improvements are substantial in several settings; for example, Table 20 shows GCN Macro-F1 gains of 3.77 points on Cora and 8.13 points on CiteSeer over the strongest listed baselines.
Analyses of pseudo-label accuracy, clustering/classifier agreement, and performance across imbalance levels provide useful diagnostic evidence beyond aggregate classification results.

Pseudocode, optimization settings, hyperparameter ranges, public benchmarks, and a code URL provide a useful foundation for reproduction. No material ethical concerns are apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: The central entropy theorem is not established. Appendix C drops the unequal class priors and class-specific concentrations introduced in Section 3, replaces individual distances with aggregate quantities without justification, and derives contradictory bounds. At D_intra = 0, its final inequalities require both H >= log C and H <= log C - kappa/(2C^2). More generally, moving an embedding toward an incorrect class center can increase the proposed geometric-imbalance score while decreasing entropy through confident misclassification.

Theorem 2 conflates imbalance in labeled training samples with neighborhood composition. Subsampling labels on a fixed graph does not imply that minority nodes acquire more majority neighbors; with a fixed encoder and class centers, existing embeddings remain unchanged. Appendix D assumes the necessary relationship between neighborhood mixing and imbalance, then changes a claimed dependence on rho squared into proportionality to rho. A graph-generating model and valid additional assumptions are needed.

The connection between the theory and implementation remains weak. DGIS uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest centroid margin, whereas Definition 1 measures distance to the true class center relative to global separation; no approximation guarantee or direct validation connects them. The ranking explanation is also inaccurate: the confidence weight min(r, 1-r) decreases once r exceeds 0.5. Theorem 3 establishes an algebraic weighting property, not a guarantee of reduced geometric imbalance or pseudo-label error.

The component evaluation contains material contradictions. As printed, Tables 1 and 32 give the highest F1 in every setting to configurations marked as excluding both Node-Reordering and DGIS, contradicting the accompanying claim that their combination performs best. There is no clearly labeled configuration enabling all components. Tables 17 and 27 also report different UNREAL results for ostensibly the same ogbn-arxiv setting, including GCN F1 values of 50.32 and 50.65. These inconsistencies prevent confident interpretation of the evidence.

Originality relative to closely related self-training methods is insufficiently established. Appendix B already describes M3S as filtering pseudo-labels through clustering/classifier agreement, closely resembling DPAM, yet the direct comparison is restricted to CS-Random. IceBerg is discussed but not evaluated. Broader comparisons under matched training and tuning budgets would clarify the contribution of the added ranking and filtering mechanisms.

The scalability and reproducibility claims exceed the supplied details. Appendix K omits comparable hyperparameter configurations for ogbn-arxiv/products and does not adequately specify the large-scale sampling setup. Table 12 measures fixed training epochs and selection operations on small graphs, while the complete method can use 100 retraining rounds. End-to-end runtime, peak memory, and matched computational budgets are needed to substantiate the efficiency claims. These gaps, together with the invalid central theory and inconsistent ablations, outweigh the promising reported gains.
